Marie Curie (born Maria Salomea Skłodowska) was a pioneering Polish-French physicist and chemist. She is renowned for her groundbreaking research on radioactivity, a term she coined.

Throughout her career, she achieved numerous historical milestones, including becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, the only woman to win two Nobel Prizes, and the only person to win a Nobel Prize in two different scientific fields (Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911). Her work included the discovery of the elements polonium and radium and the development of techniques for isolating radioactive isotopes.

Beyond her laboratory work, she championed the use of portable X-ray units to treat wounded soldiers during World War I. Her legacy continues to influence scientific research and medical applications today, although her prolonged exposure to radiation ultimately led to her death in 1934.
